rationale: The printed entry identifies 'love' (specifically 'the love of God' as the phrase is used of human beings toward God) as the keeping of His commandments, and the three texts printed with the entry state that identification almost verbatim: 1 John 5:3 ('this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments'), John 14:15 ('If ye love me, keep my commandments'), and 2 John 6 ('this is love, that we walk after his commandments'). The 'this is... that (hina)' formula in the Johannine epistles is naturally epexegetical/definitional, so the entry is not extrapolating but transcribing. The book further shows the identification is not a Johannine novelty: Deuteronomy 6:5 with 10:12-13 and Exodus 20:6 pair 'them that love me' with 'and keep my commandments,' and Romans 13:10 states 'love is the fulfilling of the law.' The strongest counter — that love is an inner self-giving disposition of which obedience is merely the evidence or fruit — reads John 14:15 plausibly but must treat the explicit definitional formulas of 1 John 5:3 and 2 John 6 as loose speech, and it supplies no text the book's identification cannot absorb. The counter's best exhibit, 1 Cor 13:3 (deeds without love profit nothing), is answered by the book's Saul/1 Samuel 15:22 distinction between self-chosen offerings and commanded obedience, and by Paul's own catalog, which itemizes commandments ('does not envy... worketh no ill to his neighbour: therefore love is the fulfilling of the law'). Since no specific alternative explains the supplied texts with fewer unsupported steps, the entry stands, with the affective-exclusion elaboration noted as contestable but secondary.
book_core_identification: In Scripture's own usage, the love of God (humanity's love toward God, and love of neighbor under Him) is enacted commandment-keeping — obedience to what God commanded — rather than an inner feeling or mere affection: 'this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments' (1 John 5:3).
book_secondary_elaborations: The strict-identity claim that love is 'not a reason to obey; it is the keeping itself' (obedience is the love, not merely its expression or evidence)
The four-office scheme aligning love, knowing, faith, and belief as distinct offices of the one act of keeping commandments
The reading of 1 Corinthians 13 as a 'legal argument' itemizing commandments, with the 'mirror' of v.12 identified as the law via James 1:23-25
The treatment of biblical 'hate' as covenantal un-choosing (Leah, Luke 14:26/Matthew 10:37, Hosea 9:15) rather than emotional hostility
The claim that the commandment defining love is 'from the beginning' (archē) and therefore as old as creation
The pairing of the two great commandments with the two tables of the Decalogue
strongest_counter_interpretation: Love is fundamentally an inner disposition of self-giving devotion — grounded in God's own agape nature (1 John 4:8; John 3:16; Romans 5:8) — and commandment-keeping is the necessary evidence, fruit, or expression of that disposition, not its definition. On this reading John 14:15 makes love the antecedent condition and obedience its consequence ('if ye love me, [then] keep my commandments'), Deuteronomy 6:5's 'with all thine heart, and with all thy soul' locates love in the inner person, and 1 Corinthians 13:3 proves love is distinguishable from outward deeds, since one can give all goods to the poor and one's body to be burned and still 'have not love.'
counter_core_identification: Love = an inner, self-giving covenantal disposition toward God and neighbor, of which obedience to the commandments is the outward expression and proof rather than the thing itself.
material_core_denial: The counter denies that keeping the commandments IS the love of God; it holds that love is a prior interior devotion that produces keeping, so that 1 John 5:3's formula describes love's manifestation rather than its definition, and that the book collapses the motive into its fruit.
counter_case: John 14:15's conditional grammar distinguishes love (the condition) from keeping (the commanded result), suggesting two related but non-identical things
Deuteronomy 6:5 commands love 'with all thine heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy might' — interior language ill-suited to a purely behavioral definition
1 Corinthians 13:3 explicitly imagines maximal outward deeds ('bestow all my goods to feed the poor... give my body to be burned') performed without love, so love cannot simply be doing
Mainstream usage of 1 John 4:7-10 makes love first God's own nature and initiative ('herein is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us'), prior to any human obedience
Matthew 22:40 says the law 'hangs' on love, arguably making love the source from which commandments derive rather than the commandments themselves
book_explanatory_advantages: The three printed texts use explicit definitional formulas ('this is the love of God, that...'; 'this is love, that we walk after his commandments'), which the book takes at face value and the counter must soften

The Old Testament idiom independently corroborates the identification: Exodus 20:6 and Deuteronomy 10:12-13 / 6:5 pair loving God with keeping His commandments as one covenantal stance, and 2 John expressly says the commandment is 'from the beginning,' not new

Romans 13:8-10 ('love worketh no ill to his neighbour: therefore love is the fulfilling of the law') and 1 Timothy 1:5 ('the purpose of the commandment is love') give the same commandment-shaped definition in Paul

The book explains the Matthew 7:22-23 / 1 Corinthians 13 convergence precisely: Paul's 'without love' and Jesus' 'ye that work lawlessness (anomia)' name the same deficiency from two sides — spectacular gifts minus commandment-keeping — which the dispositional reading leaves as coincidence

1 Samuel 15:22 supplies the category the counter's 1 Cor 13:3 objection needs: self-chosen sacrifices (goods given, body burned) are offerings in place of the command, so deeds without love are deeds without the commandments kept, not a refutation of the identification
The book's reading of biblical love/hate as covenantal choosing/un-choosing (Genesis 29:30-31; Luke 14:26 vs Matthew 10:37; Exodus 20:5-6) resolves texts that embarrass an emotional definition
counter_explanatory_advantages: John 14:15's conditional syntax reads most naturally as love preceding and motivating obedience
Deuteronomy 6:5's heart/soul/might language and Matthew 22:37 preserve an affective, whole-person dimension the book's behavioral definition risks flattening
1 Corinthians 13:3 shows Scripture itself can conceive of outward deeds without love, which fits a disposition-plus-expression model straightforwardly
The counter integrates God's own love (John 3:16; 1 John 4:9-10; Romans 5:8) and human love under one definition, whereas the entry addresses only the human-toward-God direction
decisive_sources: 1 John 5:3 — the entry's identification stated as a definition in the text itself
2 John 4-6 — 'this is love, that we walk after his commandments,' with the commandment 'from the beginning'
John 14:15 — love toward Christ cashed out as keeping His commandments
Exodus 20:5-6 with Deuteronomy 6:5; 10:12-13 — the Old Testament covenant idiom pairing 'them that love me' with 'keep my commandments'
Romans 13:8-10 — 'love is the fulfilling of the law,' independent Pauline attestation of the commandment-shaped definition
Matthew 7:22-23 read against 1 Corinthians 13:1-3 — gifts without love / powers with lawlessness as the same audit, explained only if love = commandments kept
unresolved_objections: The strict-identity elaboration ('love is not a reason to obey; it is the keeping itself') goes beyond what the texts strictly require; an inseparable disposition-and-enactment reading remains grammatically possible for John 14:15 and Deuteronomy 6:5's heart-language, though it does not overturn the core referent

The entry's definition covers human love toward God and neighbor; it does not account for (nor claim to account for) the Godward direction of 1 John 4:8-10 and John 3:16, which the common interpretation makes primary — the two treat partially different scopes of the word
Whether 'the love of God' in 1 John 5:3 is an objective genitive (our love for God) is assumed rather than argued, though context (5:2) supports it
The 1 Cor 13:12 'mirror = law' identification via James 1:23-25 is an ingenious but non-necessary secondary link
